alternatives: Lamotrigine: not associated with hyperammonemia; cleared by hepatic glucuronidation, so titrate slowly (rash and Stevens-Johnson risk) and reduce the dose in moderate to severe hepatic impairment
Lithium: renally cleared and not hepatotoxic, but needs level monitoring and no thiazide
contraindications: Valproate in hepatic encephalopathy and decompensated liver disease: avoid (hyperammonemia, hepatotoxicity)
interactions: Valproate impairs urea-cycle function (reduced N-acetylglutamate activation of carbamoyl phosphate synthetase I) and depletes carnitine, raising ammonia even without liver disease and at therapeutic levels
In cirrhosis, reduced hepatic urea-cycle capacity amplifies valproate-associated hyperammonemia; hypoalbuminemia raises the free valproate fraction, so the total level understates exposure
output.proposed: Valproate (divalproex sodium) 500 mg twice daily in Child-Pugh B cirrhosis with hepatic encephalopathy; with lithium, quetiapine, amlodipine and hydrochlorothiazide
warnings: Stopping valproate in bipolar disorder risks a mood episode; plan the replacement with psychiatry
L-carnitine supplementation is used to treat valproate-associated hyperammonemia

alternatives: Replace the thiazide with an antihypertensive that does not alter lithium clearance, such as a higher amlodipine dose
contraindications: Thiazide with lithium without dose reduction and close level monitoring
interactions: Thiazide diuretics reduce renal lithium clearance by about 25-40%, raising the level within days to weeks of starting; a well-documented cause of lithium toxicity
Hyponatremia and volume depletion (diuretics, poor intake, lactulose-induced diarrhea) increase proximal tubular lithium reabsorption and raise the level further
Lactulose and rifaximin: no direct pharmacokinetic interaction with lithium; the risk is indirect, through fluid and sodium loss
output.proposed: Lithium carbonate 600 mg twice daily with hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily; lactulose to be started
warnings: Lithium toxicity (coarse tremor, ataxia, confusion) overlaps with encephalopathy; recheck the level whenever a diuretic, NSAID or ACE inhibitor is started
Monitor lithium level, sodium, creatinine and fluid balance while lactulose is titrated

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Lithium 1.6 mEq/L and valproate 118 µg/mL above their therapeutic ranges; serum ethanol 22 mg/dL; sodium 134 mEq/L; bilirubin 2.4 mg/dL, albumin 2.8 g/dL, INR 1.6, platelets 94 x10^9/L; creatinine, CRP and white cell count normal; ammonia 76 µmol/L supportive only
action_criteria.label: Core laboratory work-up: blood count, electrolytes, renal and liver function, glucose, INR, ammonia and CRP, with toxicology where alcohol or drugs are in question; here also lithium and valproate levels
action_criteria.rationale: Confirms liver dysfunction and identifies metabolic and infective precipitants; lithium and valproate levels and ethanol are needed because all three are candidate precipitants [ACG_HE_2026]

action_criteria.rationale: Infection is the commonest precipitant of overt HE and can be occult in cirrhosis; this patient is afebrile with a normal white cell count and no focal source, so the screen is recommended rather than required (EASL 2022).

action_criteria.rationale: Infection is the commonest precipitant of overt HE and can be occult in cirrhosis; this patient is afebrile with a normal white cell count and no focal source, so the screen is recommended rather than required (EASL 2022).

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Valproate raises ammonia through urea-cycle inhibition, amplified in cirrhosis; hydrochlorothiazide reduces lithium clearance, and lactulose-induced fluid loss can raise the lithium level further
action_criteria.label: Medication review of valproate in cirrhosis and of lithium with hydrochlorothiazide, with quetiapine and lactulose
action_criteria.rationale: Valproate-associated hyperammonemia and the thiazide-lithium interaction are precipitants, so stopping valproate, holding lithium, replacing the thiazide and watching lithium during lactulose change management [ACG_HE_2026]

prohibited_recommendations: Do not give benzodiazepines or other sedatives for agitation or sleep: they precipitate and prolong hepatic encephalopathy; manage agitation with reorientation, a safe environment and treatment of the precipitant (EASL 2022).
Do not prescribe sedating opioids, which worsen hepatic encephalopathy; use acetaminophen up to 2 g per day for pain.
Do not restart valproate: it caused hyperammonemia here and is hepatotoxic in cirrhosis.
Do not continue hydrochlorothiazide with lithium: thiazides reduce lithium clearance and precipitated this toxicity.
Do not treat the presentation as mania with an added antipsychotic or a higher mood-stabilizer dose; haloperidol is also excluded by her documented dystonic reaction.
required_recommendations: Stop valproate and do not restart it; give IV L-carnitine for valproate-associated hyperammonemia (100 mg/kg loading dose, maximum 6 g, then 15 mg/kg every 4 hours).

Hold lithium and stop hydrochlorothiazide; give isotonic saline to restore volume and lithium clearance with fluid-balance monitoring, repeat the lithium level with sodium and creatinine every 6-12 hours, and involve nephrology or toxicology for extracorporeal removal if the level rises, kidney function worsens or consciousness falls despite fluids (EXTRIP 2015).

Lactulose 25 mL every 1-2 hours until at least two soft bowel movements, then titrated to 2-3 soft bowel movements per day (ACG 2026 recommendation 10; EASL 2022); avoid over-titration, which causes dehydration, hypokalemia and kidney injury (and here would raise the lithium level).
Give parenteral thiamine before any glucose, and monitor for alcohol withdrawal (CIWA-Ar) given nightly drinking and a detectable ethanol.

Psychiatry review of the bipolar regimen: valproate is not restarted, quetiapine is held while she is encephalopathic, lithium is resumed only at a reduced dose once the level is normal and without a thiazide, and any alternative such as lamotrigine is titrated slowly at a dose adjusted for hepatic impairment.
Replace hydrochlorothiazide with an antihypertensive that does not alter lithium clearance, for example a higher amlodipine dose.

Refer for liver transplant assessment (decompensated cirrhosis with overt HE, MELD-Na 18; EASL 2018) together with treatment of alcohol-use disorder, since abstinence determines prognosis and candidacy.

avoided_actions.rationale: No clinical suspicion for hepatopulmonary syndrome, portopulmonary hypertension, or endocarditis; echocardiography is not part of the HE workup.
Amyloid PET has no role in HE workup; reversible metabolic encephalopathy is the issue, not Alzheimer pathology.
DaTscan has no role in HE workup; the question is metabolic encephalopathy, not nigrostriatal degeneration.
Early-onset AD genetic panel has no role in HE workup; reversible metabolic encephalopathy is the diagnosis under consideration.

accepted: Hepatic encephalopathy (West Haven grade II), alcoholic cirrhosis (Child-Pugh B, MELD-Na 18), with multiple drug and alcohol precipitants: (1) valproate-induced hyperammonemia (level 118 µg/mL), (2) lithium toxicity (1.6 mEq/L) after hydrochlorothiazide was added, (3) quetiapine CNS depression, and (4) recent alcohol use (ethanol 22 mg/dL).

differential.key_features: Pressured speech and flight of ideas resemble her prior manic episodes, but asterixis, disorientation and diffuse theta slowing on EEG indicate an encephalopathy; mania does not cause asterixis or slow the EEG.

Level 1.6 mEq/L (mild toxicity) three weeks after hydrochlorothiazide was added, with tremor and ataxia; it contributes, but hyperammonemia on valproate in decompensated cirrhosis is also present, so it is not the whole explanation.

Valproate 118 µg/mL (free fraction higher with albumin 2.8 g/dL) impairs the urea cycle and raises ammonia independently of liver function; in cirrhosis the effect is amplified; it is one precipitant here, together with lithium toxicity.

Nightly drinking, tachycardia 104 and tremor fit early withdrawal, but ethanol is still detectable (22 mg/dL), there is no diaphoresis or hallucination, and asterixis is not a withdrawal sign; monitor with CIWA-Ar.
Daily drinker with confusion and ataxia, but extraocular movements are full without nystagmus, and the ataxia and tremor are explained by lithium toxicity; parenteral thiamine is given empirically.

key_clinical_evidence: HE is a clinical diagnosis: West Haven grade, evidence of liver disease and exclusion of other causes of altered mental status.

An elevated ammonia neither grades nor confirms hepatic encephalopathy and repeat levels are not used to guide treatment; a normal ammonia in a confused patient with cirrhosis should prompt a search for another cause (ACG 2026 recommendation 5 and key concept 14; EASL 2022).
Child-Pugh B (8: bilirubin 2.4 2, albumin 2.8 2, INR 1.6 1, no ascites 1, HE grade 2 2); MELD-Na 18 (creatinine 1.1, bilirubin 2.4, INR 1.6, sodium 134)

Precipitant identification is more actionable than the ammonia number: infection (SBP especially), GI bleed, electrolyte disturbance (hypokalemia/hyponatremia), constipation, sedative/CNS-depressant use, dehydration, dietary protein load, renal failure.
Valproate can produce hyperammonemic encephalopathy in patients without liver disease (urea-cycle inhibition); in cirrhosis the effect is potentiated. L-carnitine supplementation is used to treat it.
Thiazides reduce lithium clearance; the lithium-HCTZ combination is a well-known cause of toxicity.
Mania does not cause asterixis or diffuse EEG slowing; these findings point to an encephalopathy even in a patient with a psychiatric history.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Asterixis, disorientation and diffuse EEG slowing in cirrhosis, with hyperammonemia on valproate and a toxic lithium level, indicate a metabolic encephalopathy with a behavioral overlay, not primary mania.
red_herrings.data_point: Acute manic-appearing presentation in known bipolar
red_herrings.intended_effect: Anchor on bipolar relapse and add antipsychotic; miss multifactorial metabolic precipitants.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Ethanol 22 mg/dL is well below intoxication; it confirms recent drinking (a contributor, and a reason for thiamine and withdrawal monitoring), but the dominant drivers are valproate, lithium and cirrhosis.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Attribute presentation to recent alcohol use.

metadata.difficulty_description: Diagnostic puzzle: a bipolar patient whose encephalopathy mimics mania; valproate-associated hyperammonemia (urea-cycle inhibition) as a primary precipitant, concurrent lithium toxicity after a thiazide was added, and recent alcohol use; asterixis and EEG slowing are the findings that discriminate against primary mania.
metadata.difficulty_rationale: Two required steps (core labs with lithium, valproate and ethanol levels; medication review of valproate and of lithium with hydrochlorothiazide); several simultaneous contributors; the psychiatric overlay creates anchoring risk.

patient.history_present_illness: Ms. W. is a 52-year-old woman with bipolar disorder type I and unacknowledged alcoholic cirrhosis who was brought to the ED by her sister for acute confusion and 'weird behavior' over the prior 24 hours. Her sister describes pressured speech, disorganized thinking, limited sleep, and running out of her apartment to 'check on the neighbors' repeatedly, behaviors that appear similar to prior manic episodes. The patient was last psychiatrically hospitalized 2 years ago for a manic episode. She takes lithium, valproate and quetiapine for bipolar disorder and is adherent with her medications per sister. Her primary care physician added hydrochlorothiazide for hypertension 3 weeks ago.
